name: OpenSSH scp
summary: The OpenSSH scp file-copy client, which parses local and remote operands, establishes SSH-backed sessions, and in current OpenSSH uses the SFTP protocol by default while retaining a legacy SCP mode.

features.name: SSH-backed copy orchestration
features.description: scp parses source and target operands, starts ssh or sftp-backed connections, and routes local/remote copy direction through distinct source and sink functions. The copy client delegates peer authentication and encrypted transport to OpenSSH session setup.
benefits: Reuses SSH authentication and transport configuration
Keeps local operand parsing and copy policy in one command boundary
costs: Copy behavior inherits SSH configuration and remote execution assumptions
Local/remote direction and multiple operands expand lifecycle paths

features.name: SFTP default transfer path
features.description: At the pinned OpenSSH revision, scp opens an SFTP connection for ordinary operation and uses SFTP client operations for source and sink transfer. The -O option selects the legacy SCP protocol path instead.
benefits: Uses a structured file-transfer subsystem for current interoperability
Preserves an explicit compatibility route for older SCP servers
costs: Two protocol paths require separate behavior and compatibility testing
The command name alone does not identify which wire protocol is used

features.name: Recursive source and sink copy
features.description: scp maintains recursive source traversal and sink handling, including directory targets, metadata options, and local-to-remote, remote-to-local, and remote-to-remote orchestration. The pinned source keeps SFTP and legacy protocol copy functions separate.
benefits: Provides a familiar tree-copy boundary for remote filesystems
Makes copy direction and recursive behavior explicit in command state
costs: Remote path and metadata semantics depend on server filesystem permissions
Recursive and remote-to-remote cases add multiple connection and failure paths

mathematical_views.question: How do parsed operands select local, remote-shell, SFTP, legacy SCP, and copy-direction states?
assumptions: Operands are classified as local or remote endpoint descriptions
Mode flags choose SFTP or legacy SCP behavior
The view abstracts shell quoting and SSH cryptographic negotiation

mathematical_views.question: How are local files, remote sessions, SFTP handles, and destination sinks connected for a copy operation?
assumptions: Source and sink are distinct endpoints even for remote-to-remote copies
Edges represent stream or SFTP operations and do not guarantee successful persistence
Recursive traversal is modeled as expansion of source nodes

benefits: SSH identity, host-key, and transport configuration reuse
costs: Copy lifecycle depends on SSH session setup and remote permissions

benefits: Structured current transfer path with legacy compatibility
costs: Maintaining two protocol paths complicates semantics and testing
Tree traversal and remote metadata failures can be partial and difficult to reason about
